thread:
maya: Quick question — we flipped service X to an NLB with TLS on port 443 via Terraform and health checks are failing (targets go UNHEALTHY). No app code change. Any quick config checks?

maya: Terraform snippet we used: `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: \"nlb\"`, `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-ssl-ports: \"https\"`, and `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-ssl-cert: \"arn:aws:acm:...\"`. Service port name is `https` and containerPort=8443.

maya: Errors in ELB health: `Health check failed: HTTP 503` (we expected TLS passthrough -> TCP).

sanjay: Did you change target type? For nlb + TLS passthrough we usually use `nlb-ip` + TCP health checks. If you configured SSL ports on the load balancer it terminates TLS and then uses HTTP health checks on target group — mismatch if your pod speaks TLS or expects SNI.

sanjay: Quick checklist:
- port name on Service must match annotation port name (`https`)
- `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: \"nlb\"` vs `nlb-ip` (nlb vs nlb-ip changes target type)
- health check protocol/port on the target group (HTTP vs TCP)
- externalTrafficPolicy: Local vs Cluster (for source IP sticky health)

leo: Another gotcha: when you set `aws-load-balancer-ssl-ports` the controller creates a TLS listener and a target group with protocol HTTP by default (it terminates cert on LB). If your pod expects TLS you need to either:
- stop LB from terminating TLS (don't set ssl-ports / use TCP listener), or
- keep TLS termination and make pods speak plain HTTP on target group port.

leo: For Terraform (aws_lb_target_group) we usually explicitly set `protocol = \"TCP\"` and `health_check { protocol = \"TCP\" }` for passthrough. Example snippet:```hcl
resource \"aws_lb_target_group\" \"app\" {
  name     = \"app-nlb-tg\"
  port     = 443
  protocol = \"TCP\"
  vpc_id   = var.vpc_id
  target_type = \"ip\"
  health_check {
    protocol = \"TCP\"
    port     = \"traffic-port\"
  }
}
```

olivia: On the k8s side, try `kubectl describe svc my-app -n prod` and `kubectl get endpoints my-app -n prod -o yaml` to ensure endpoints exist and are the right ports. Also check pod readiness probe path vs LB healthcheck path mismatch.

maya: Running those now: endpoints look fine, pods ready. readiness probe is `HTTP /readyz` on 8443 (TLS).

sanjay: If readiness probe is HTTP on TLS port you'll need LB to talk HTTP (terminate TLS) or change probe to TCP or use a sidecar that terminates TLS. Easiest short-term: change target group's health check protocol to TCP so it doesn't send HTTP and fail with 503.

maya: Good call. Where do I change target group attrs from k8s -> terraform? We used the aws-load-balancer annotations only and let AWS controller create TG.

leo: If you rely on the AWS controller (service annotations) you can add: `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-protocol: \"tcp\"` and `service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-healthcheck-port: \"traffic-port\"`. For NLB that should force TCP health checks. If that doesn't expose the annotation your controller may not support it — then author the TG in terraform and reference it (more work).

olivia: Also check `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` so node-level healthchecks reflect pod readiness (prevents kube-proxy from hiding endpoints). But Local means you need nodePort on nodes with pods.

maya: Trying annotation change now, then I'll `kubectl annotate svc my-app ... && kubectl patch svc` to trigger reconcile.
